This article is about the 1994 Australian novel. For the poem by the same name, see [Dylan Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Thomas "Dylan Thomas").
The Hand That Signed the Paper
AuthorHelen Demidenko
LanguageEnglish
GenreFiction
PublisherAllen & Unwin

Publication date

1994
Publication placeAustralia
Media typePrint
Pages157
ISBN978-1-86373-654-1
OCLC1510153690
_**The Hand That Signed the Paper**_ is a 1994 novel and [literary hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_hoax "Literary hoax"). The novel was written by Helen Darville, now [Helen Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Dale "Helen Dale"), and was published under the name Helen Demidenko. It tells the story of a Ukrainian family that collaborated with [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") during [the Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust"). The novel initially received a positive reception and was the 1995 winner of Australia's top literary prize, the [Miles Franklin Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Franklin_Award "Miles Franklin Award"). But it soon became the subject of a heated debate—first over accusations of antisemitism, followed by the revelation that Darville had adopted a false identity to imply that the novel was based on her own family history. The novel is narrated by Fiona Kovalenko, a university student of Irish-Ukrainian descent living in [Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland "Queensland"), Australia. Fiona's uncle Vitaly has been charged with [crimes against humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimes_against_humanity "Crimes against humanity") for his service as a guard at the [Treblinka extermination camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treblinka_extermination_camp "Treblinka extermination camp"). The novel recounts Vitaly and his siblings' upbringing in Ukraine amid the [Holodomor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor "Holodomor"), positing that Jewish involvement in [Bolshevism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolshevism "Bolshevism") was a motive for [Ukrainian participation in the Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_collaboration_with_Nazi_Germany "Ukrainian collaboration with Nazi Germany"). The novel also explores the moral responsibility of the Holocaust's perpetrators, and suggests that it is unjust to prosecute Nazi collaborators like Fiona's father and uncle for actions taken during the war. Helen Darville, the daughter of middle-class English parents, presented herself as a working-class Irish-Ukrainian woman named Helen Demidenko between around the time she began writing the novel as a student at the [University of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland") in 1992 and her eventual exposure in 1995. The unpublished manuscript was the winner of the 1993 [_The Australian_/Vogel Literary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Australian/Vogel_Literary_Award "The Australian/Vogel Literary Award") and was published by [Allen & Unwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_%26_Unwin "Allen & Unwin") in August 1994. The novel received a positive reception upon its release and was the winner of the 1995 Miles Franklin Award and [ALS Gold Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALS_Gold_Medal "ALS Gold Medal"). But it then began to attract criticism over accusations that it was overly sympathetic towards the perpetrators of the Holocaust. The backlash intensified in August 1995 when it was revealed that "Helen Demidenko" was a fabrication and that Darville had no familial connection to Ukraine. The controversy surrounding the novel has been the subject of multiple books, including [Andrew Riemer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Riemer "Andrew Riemer")'s _The Demidenko Debate_ and [Robert Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Manne "Robert Manne")'s _The Culture of Forgetting_. Defenders of the novel have argued that it is a worthy experiment in [postmodern fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodern_literature "Postmodern literature"), while critics have contended that it is an antisemitic work and that it distorts the history and moral lessons of the Holocaust. [![Image 2: Two people walk down a paved street while bodies lie on the footpath behind them.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/HolodomorKharkiv_1933_Wienerberger.jpg/250px-HolodomorKharkiv_1933_Wienerberger.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HolodomorKharkiv_1933_Wienerberger.jpg) Starved peasants on a street in [Kharkiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kharkiv "Kharkiv"), Ukraine, in 1933 Fiona Kovalenko, the daughter of an Irish mother and Ukrainian father, is a university student in [Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland "Queensland"), Australia. Her uncle Vitaly immigrated to Australia from Ukraine in 1948 and has recently been charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity for his role in [the Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust"). Fiona fears that her father Evheny may also be charged. Fiona describes finding photos in her father's bedside table at the age of 12 showing her father and uncle in [SS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS "SS") uniforms participating in the massacre of Jews at [Babi Yar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babi_Yar "Babi Yar") and guarding prisoners at the [Treblinka extermination camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treblinka_extermination_camp "Treblinka extermination camp"). Kateryna, the sister of Vitaly and Evheny, begins describing her upbringing in a village near [Khmel'nik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmilnyk "Khmilnyk"), Ukraine. She recounts the 1930s famine known as the [Holodomor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor "Holodomor") and the repression that Ukraine suffered under the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). During the famine the [kommisar's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissar "Commissar") wife, a Jewish doctor named Judit, refuses to treat Kateryna's youngest brother and likens Ukrainians to dogs. The famine eventually takes the lives of Kateryna's brother and all 12 of her cousins. Kateryna and Evheny are sent away to a [Komsomol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komsomol "Komsomol") school, although Evheny quickly runs away. At the school Kateryna blames the famine on "communists and Jews" and is told by her fellow Ukrainian students that [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") will help them to get revenge. Following [the German invasion of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa "Operation Barbarossa"), the village's residents begin to massacre communists. The [German Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Army_/(1935%E2%80%931945/) "German Army (1935–1945)") arrives in the village and is joyfully welcomed by its inhabitants, while Kateryna and her fellow students are evacuated to [Kiev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyiv "Kyiv") as German troops surround the city. On the journey she develops a connection with a German [SS captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauptsturmf%C3%BChrer "Hauptsturmführer") named Wilhelm Hasse, with whom she enters into a relationship. Vitaly and Evheny join many of the other young men from their village in signing up to join the SS as [auxiliary volunteers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiwi_/(volunteer/) "Hiwi (volunteer)"). In Kiev, Kateryna watches from a window as two uniformed men rape and kill a Jewish woman. She recognises one of the men as Evheny and waves to him. The next day, the Jews of Kiev are marched to the Babi Yar ravine and massacred using machine guns. [![Image 3: Two uniformed men holding rifles stand in front of a doorway amid rubble and debris. Inside the doorway are multiple bodies.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Askaris_im_Warschauer_Getto_-_1943.jpg/250px-Askaris_im_Warschauer_Getto_-_1943.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Askaris_im_Warschauer_Getto_-_1943.jpg) Ukrainian members of the SS standing in front of Jewish corpses in the [Warsaw Ghetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Ghetto "Warsaw Ghetto") Vitaly is assigned to the [Warsaw Ghetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Ghetto "Warsaw Ghetto") and recalls bayonetting a Jewish baby hidden in a knapsack before shooting the father. He is later reassigned to Treblinka, where he is tasked with burning the corpses of those who have been killed in the gas chambers and participates in the looting of their belongings. He describes throwing infants into the air so that another guard, known as [Ivan the Terrible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_the_Terrible_/(Treblinka_guard/) "Ivan the Terrible (Treblinka guard)"), could catch them on a bayonet. A guard explains that Ivan is particularly brutal towards the prisoners because during the famine Jews burned down his house while his parents and six siblings were trapped inside. Vitaly begins a relationship with a Polish girl named Magda and has a son named Ihor. Eventually, following a [prisoner revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treblinka_uprising "Treblinka uprising"), the Treblinka camp is shut down and Vitaly is sent to the front, leaving Magda and Ihor behind in Poland. Evheny, serving with the [14th Waffen SS Galizien Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14th_Waffen_Grenadier_Division_of_the_SS_/(1st_Galician/) "14th Waffen Grenadier Division of the SS (1st Galician)"), surrenders to the British at [Klagenfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klagenfurt_am_W%C3%B6rthersee "Klagenfurt am Wörthersee") in 1945. He migrates to Britain with Kateryna, whose husband Hasse was killed in the [Battle of Stalingrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad "Battle of Stalingrad"). They learn that their mother was killed in an industrial accident while [working as a forced labourer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labour_under_German_rule_during_World_War_II "Forced labour under German rule during World War II") in Germany. They assume that Vitaly is also dead and are preparing to move to Canada until they learn in 1949 that he has migrated to Australia and is working on the [Snowy Mountains Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowy_Mountains_Scheme "Snowy Mountains Scheme"). Evheny, his Irish fiancée Margaret, Kateryna, and Kateryna's two children all move to Australia to join him. In the present day, as Fiona works to help Vitaly prepare for his trial, he dies in hospital from a stroke. Fiona continues to protest the ongoing war crimes trials, but her father is ultimately not charged. Fiona visits Treblinka where she meets a man whose [Quaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaker "Quaker") aunt was killed at the camp. He asks her whether she is sorry for what her uncle did, and she says that she is. Helen Darville, the author of _The Hand That Signed the Paper_, grew up in Queensland, Australia, as the daughter of two middle-class English migrants, Harry and Grace Darville.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne19964-1) She attended [Redeemer Lutheran College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redeemer_Lutheran_College "Redeemer Lutheran College") in [Rochedale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochedale,_Queensland "Rochedale, Queensland"), a suburb of [Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne19965%E2%80%936-2) In 1989 Darville began her university studies at the [University of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"), where she quickly developed a reputation as a fabulist.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199613%E2%80%9315-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobertsMakler1995-4) She initially introduced herself as being of upper-class Belgian or Franco-Norman descent and claimed to be a graduate of one of Brisbane's most prestigious private schools. She also claimed to be a prodigious mathematician and the daughter of a Czech resistance fighter. Eventually Darville settled on the story that she was the daughter of a working-class Irish mother and Ukrainian father.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199615%E2%80%9316-5) Around the middle of 1992 Darville began using the surname Demidenko-Darville, before eventually adopting the surname Demidenko. Around the same time, she began working on the manuscript for _The Hand That Signed the Paper_.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199617,_20-6) Darville's manuscript was initially written as a work of non-fiction, with its characters sharing her adopted surname. An author's note claimed that the work was based on interviews with her supposed uncle Vitaly Demidenko.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox2005-7) Darville's boyfriend Paul Gadaloff later claimed that Darville had become obsessed with the notion of Jewish control of society and with the [Jewish Bolshevism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Bolshevism "Jewish Bolshevism") conspiracy theory.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199620%E2%80%9322-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoutsoukis1995-9) He also claimed that Darville had described her book as a work of oral history, telling him that her uncle Vitaly lived in Adelaide and that he had been a guard at Treblinka.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199623-10) A friend of Darville's, [Natalie Jane Prior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Jane_Prior "Natalie Jane Prior"), later wrote that Darville had a tendency during this period to use "ugly, offensive and tiresome" language about "hook-nosed Jews and looney Zionists".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199620-11) Darville's manuscript was written amid a nationwide debate over the trials of Nazi war criminals in [South Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Australia "South Australia"). In 1988, the Australian government had passed the War Crimes Amendment Act to allow for the prosecution of the estimated 4000–5000 war criminals who had moved to Australia following the Second World War.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019285-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGunew1996a3-13) The act was controversial, with many fearing that the legislation would result in costly and socially divisive trials of elderly residents.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaster1995627-14) Three alleged war criminals, all Eastern European men in their seventies living in South Australia, were ultimately charged—[Ivan Polyukhovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Polyukhovich "Ivan Polyukhovich"), Mikolay Berezowsky and Heinrich Wagner—of whom only the first was brought to trial.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019285-12)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaster1995628-15) Polyukhovich was found not guilty on all charges.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaster1995628-15) [![Image 4: Two judges examining photographs of uniformed men](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Flickr_-_Government_Press_Office_%28GPO%29_-_SUPREME_COURT_JUSTICE_DOV_LEVIN_DISTRICT_AND_COURT_JUDGE_DALIA_DORNER_LOOKING_AT_A_PHOTO_ALBUM_DURING_THE_TRIAL_OF_JOHN_%28IVAN%29_DEMJANJUK.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Government_Press_Office_/(GPO/)_-_SUPREME_COURT_JUSTICE_DOV_LEVIN_DISTRICT_AND_COURT_JUDGE_DALIA_DORNER_LOOKING_AT_A_PHOTO_ALBUM_DURING_THE_TRIAL_OF_JOHN_/(IVAN/)_DEMJANJUK.jpg) Judges reviewing evidence during [John Demjanjuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Demjanjuk "John Demjanjuk")'s 1986 war crimes trial in Israel Darville was a strong opponent of the trials, later explaining, "I was very upset by the war crimes trials because I thought they were very specifically directed at the Ukrainian community and were very vindictive and sanctimonious ... it wasn't motivated by a sense of justice but by a sense of revenge".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019286-16) In 1988 Darville had written a short story in her high school magazine from the perspective of [John Demjanjuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Demjanjuk "John Demjanjuk"), who was believed at the time to be the Treblinka guard known as "Ivan the Terrible", during his war crimes trial in Israel. Her short story paints a sympathetic portrait of Demjanjuk as a victim of both Nazi Germany and the Israeli prosecution.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne19969%E2%80%9311-17) Some of Darville's acquaintances later claimed that she had also been expelled from her university's branch of the [Young Nationals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Nationals_/(Australia/) "Young Nationals (Australia)") after persistently sponsoring a motion opposing the war crimes legislation.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199614-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith201965-19) ### Manuscript development and Vogel Literary Award \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Manuscript development and Vogel Literary Award")\] In early 1993 Darville submitted her manuscript for _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ as a non-fiction work to the [University of Queensland Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Queensland_Press "University of Queensland Press"). The manuscript was rejected by the editor Sue Abbey, who wrote that she was unimpressed by its flat characters and stilted dialogue.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox2005-7) Later that year, Darville submitted the manuscript under the name Helen Demidenko to the 1993 [_The Australian_/Vogel Literary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Australian/Vogel_Literary_Award "The Australian/Vogel Literary Award"), an award for an unpublished manuscript written by an author aged under 35. The winning manuscript is awarded a publishing contract with [Allen & Unwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_%26_Unwin "Allen & Unwin").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199625-20) According to Darville, she submitted her manuscript on a whim after her brother pointed out the application form printed on a newspaper page that she had placed underneath her dogs' bowls. But Gadaloff later contradicted this account, saying that Darville had made "an assault on the Vogel from day one".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199625%E2%80%9326-21) The judges of the 1993 Vogel award were the novelist [Roger McDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_McDonald "Roger McDonald"), the fiction writer [Jennifer Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Rowe "Jennifer Rowe"), and the broadcaster [Jill Kitson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Kitson "Jill Kitson"). McDonald and Rowe did not initially see a clear favourite among the roughly sixty entries they had been sent, while Kitson quickly became a strong advocate for _The Hand That Signed the Paper_.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199631-22) Rowe was comfortable with the selection, while McDonald was more sceptical of Darville's manuscript. He sent a short report to his fellow judges expressing his reservations, including his concern that the manuscript would "be seen with justification as antisemitic".[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199632-23) McDonald later recalled that these concerns had been brushed aside by Kitson and by Patrick Gallagher, the publisher at Allen & Unwin; he eventually acceded to the decision to award the Vogel to Darville.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199633-24) The book was announced as the winner of the 1993 Vogel award on 22 September. Following the announcement, Darville—still presenting herself as Helen Demidenko—repeatedly told the media that her father had been born in Ukraine and that he had emigrated to Australia in the 1950s.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199621-25) She also told the media that she had been motivated to write her novel by the forthcoming war crimes trials.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199622-26) Representatives of her publisher, believing that the manuscript was at least in part autobiographical, were concerned that the book might put Darville's purported uncle in danger of prosecution and encouraged her to change her characters' names from "Demidenko" to "Kovalenko".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox2005-7) Darville began to describe the novel as "part fact, part fiction" and claimed that it was based "on stories and situations she had heard about from family and friends while growing up".[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199623-27) She also removed references to tape-recorded conversations with her uncle.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox2005-7) Having been awarded the right to a publishing contract, the manuscript was sent to Allen & Unwin to be edited for publication. The manuscript was first assigned to [Stephanie Dowrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Dowrick "Stephanie Dowrick"), who had edited the Vogel winners for several years. Dowrick refused to be associated with the work, later explaining that if it was not the Vogel winner she would have rejected it outright. According to Dowrick, Darville became angry at her refusal and eventually said, "the Jews are not going to get away with this one".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199634%E2%80%9336-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996114-29) The manuscript was then sent to [Brian Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Castro "Brian Castro"), who also declined to edit it and wrote, "I have no idea how this MS could have won ... I'm afraid I couldn't even finish reading it; not because of the propaganda and jingoism which abounds, and which is sometimes indistinguishable from the author's viewpoint; but because the prose is deadening and numbing."[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996114-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199637-30) Following Castro's refusal, the manuscript was sent to [Lynne Segal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynne_Segal "Lynne Segal"), who also declined to edit it.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996114-29)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199637%E2%80%9338-31) She explained privately, "By the first ten manuscript pages I started getting an inkling of what this was about. After 30 pages I decided that I could only copy edit it and let it damn itself. After 50 pages I decided to no longer work on it, and wrote a report for the publisher stating my reasons."[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199638-32) After receiving this brief report from Segal, Dowrick asked her to write a longer report detailing her concerns.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199638%E2%80%9339-33) Upon receiving Segal's report, Gallagher commissioned a retired history professor, Geoffrey Jukes, to write his own report on the manuscript's historicity.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199640-34) Jukes made some factual corrections, but concluded that the novel was largely historically accurate.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199640%E2%80%9341-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019277-36)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199669-37) The manuscript was then assigned to the editor Neil Thomas.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199643-38) Thomas later said that he had held some doubts about the novel's quality and that he had felt that it "teeter\[ed\] on the edge of apologetics".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019277-36)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199643%E2%80%9344-39) But he was satisfied by Jukes' report and agreed to edit it.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199644-40) During the editing process Darville was reluctant to make changes and expressed frustration to her acquaintances about the way the publisher was treating her.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199645%E2%80%9346-41) Darville falsely claimed to a friend that Segal and Dowrick had both been fired by Allen & Unwin after refusing to edit her manuscript.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199646%E2%80%9347-42) But despite this acrimonious relationship between Darville and her publisher, the novel was ultimately published in August 1994 with only minor changes from the Vogel-winning manuscript.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199646%E2%80%9348-43) Its back cover featured praise from the journalist [David Marr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Marr_/(journalist/) "David Marr (journalist)") and from Kitson, Darville's champion on the Vogel judging panel.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199649-44) Ahead of the publication of _The Hand That Signed the Paper_, Darville and her publisher were both bracing for the potential that the novel would spark backlash. They feared that the book would attract furore both from members of the Ukrainian community angered by the portrayal of their countrymen as war criminals, and from those in the Jewish community who would accuse the novel of providing an overly sympathetic portrayal of the Holocaust's perpetrators. Darville said in an August 1994 interview, "There's potential for a shitcan to be tipped over me with this book".[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199648-45) But despite these fears, the initial reviews were overwhelmingly positive.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199649-44) In a review in _[The Canberra Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Canberra_Times "The Canberra Times")_, Peter Pierce described the novel as "one of the most distinguished winners" of the Vogel award.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPierce1994-46) In _[The Courier-Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Courier-Mail "The Courier-Mail")_, Frank O'Shea called the novel a "fascinating and courageous piece of imaginative writing".[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199649-44) The novel was named one of the best books of 1994 by [Margaret Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Jones_/(journalist/) "Margaret Jones (journalist)") in _[The Sydney Morning Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sydney_Morning_Herald "The Sydney Morning Herald")_, where she wrote that it was "an astonishing first novel by a writer in her early 20s".[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTESydney_Morning_Herald1994-47) Reviewers reserved particular praise for the book's detached, unemotional tone.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199650%E2%80%9351-48) Reviewing the book in _[The Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Age "The Age")_, the literary critic [Andrew Riemer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Riemer "Andrew Riemer") praised the author's "precise, dispassionate prose" and wrote that Darville's aim of showing how ordinary people could commit horrific acts was both entirely legitimate and executed with great skill.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1994-49) In _The Sydney Morning Herald_, Miriam Cosic praised the author's "unflinching prose" and the novel's numb aesthetic, describing the novel as a "dense, horrifying" work.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTECosic1994-50) The early reviews were not without some suggestions of antisemitic undertones. In a review published in _[Australian Book Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Book_Review "Australian Book Review")_, Cathrine Harboe-Ree praised the work as a "fine novel", but wrote that it contained a "rather superficial view of Jews".[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarboe-Ree1994-51) In _[The Sun-Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sun-Herald "The Sun-Herald")_, [Susan Geason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Geason "Susan Geason") wrote a more sceptical review, praising the novel as an impressive debut while criticising the author's failure to properly explain her characters' motivations for collaborating with the Nazis.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeason1994-52) Riemer, despite giving an otherwise positive assessment, noted that the novel's failure to explicitly condemn its characters would likely disturb some readers.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1994-49) But these concerns were at first relatively muted.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996179-53) Darville received a mostly positive feature in _[The Australian Jewish News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Australian_Jewish_News "The Australian Jewish News")_ following the book's release, which concluded that her intentions in writing the novel were honourable.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996179-53)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlhadeff1994-54) Following the novel's publication, Darville continued to present herself as being of Ukrainian descent. She wore Ukrainian clothing in many of her public appearances, signed books in Ukrainian, and performed a Ukrainian folk dance at one event.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERyan2003216%E2%80%93217-55)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGunew1996a6-56) In a speech at the [Sydney Writers' Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Writers%27_Festival "Sydney Writers' Festival") in January 1995, Darville told the audience that she had grown up in [commission housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_housing "Public housing") and had won a scholarship to a private school, where she had graduated as [dux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dux#Education "Dux").[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199658%E2%80%9360-57) Darville claimed that her Ukrainian father Markov was a taxi driver and that her Irish mother was a domestic worker.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorley200775-58) In one interview Darville claimed that winning the Vogel award had allowed her father to take his first plane trip, and that it had been the first book her mother had ever read after leaving school at the age of 12.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTELoane1995-59) ### Miles Franklin Award \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Miles Franklin Award")\] In 1995 _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ was shortlisted for the [Miles Franklin Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Franklin_Award "Miles Franklin Award"), widely regarded as Australia's most prestigious literary award.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristoff199547-60)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennie1995-61)[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShenon1995-62) The judging panel included Kitson—who had championed the novel on the Vogel judging panel and whose praise appeared on its back cover[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199632,_49-63)—alongside the [Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_/(education/) "Chancellor (education)") of the [University of Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sydney "University of Sydney"), [Leonie Kramer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonie_Kramer "Leonie Kramer"), the head of the [State Library of New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Library_of_New_South_Wales "State Library of New South Wales"), Alison Crook, and the English professors Harry Heseltine and Adrian Mitchell.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996135%E2%80%93136-64) On 1 June, _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ was announced as the winning novel.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199665-65) In their report, the judging panel wrote that the novel "brings to light a hitherto unspeakable aspect of the Australian migrant experience" and displays "a powerful literary imagination coupled to a strong sense of history".[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennie1995-61) While the decision would not be announced until July, _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ had also been selected on 17 April as the winner of the 1995 [Australian Literature Society Gold Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALS_Gold_Medal "ALS Gold Medal").[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199662-66) Riemer later wrote that the announcement that the novel had won the Miles Franklin Award was met with "a mixture of disbelief and sardonic amusement" in literary circles.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996135-67) In his view, the novel was generally regarded as an "immature though compelling first novel" that was deserving of the Vogel award—a prize designated for emerging writers—but not the Miles Franklin.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996138%E2%80%93139-68) While some speculated that the judging panel's decision was attributable to a growing fetishisation of "multicultural chic" in Australian literature, both Riemer and the political scientist [Robert Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Manne "Robert Manne") were sceptical of this hypothesis, noting that the judging panel featured several members known for their literary conservatism.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996141%E2%80%93142-69)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199663%E2%80%9364-70) Manne ultimately concluded in his 1996 book on the saga that very little was known about the reasons for the judging panel's decision.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199664-71) ### Accusations of antisemitism \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Accusations of antisemitism")\] The eventual firestorm over Darville's novel was sparked on 9 June 1995 by the publication of a column in _The Age_ by Pamela Bone.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199671-72) The column provided a scathing assessment of the novel; Bone criticised the claim that it was "a book of extraordinary redemptive power", questioning the morality of its attempts to redeem the Holocaust's perpetrators. She also accused the novel of presenting a false historical narrative by blaming Jewish involvement in the Ukrainian famine for Ukrainian antisemitism. Bone concluded, "If Helen Demidenko condemns the antisemitism of her characters, I wish she had said so more clearly".[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBone1995a-73) On 17 June, Judith Armstrong, a professor of Russian Studies at the [University of Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Melbourne "University of Melbourne"), responded with a column defending the novel.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEArmstrong1995-74) Others soon joined the debate in _The Age_.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199673%E2%80%9375-75) The historian [Stephen G. Wheatcroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_G._Wheatcroft "Stephen G. Wheatcroft") wrote in a column on 21 June that the work contained serious historical errors and criticised Armstrong for using academic theory to validate the novel's antisemitism.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWheatcroft1995-76) Jacques Adler, a historian and former member of the [French resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_resistance "French resistance") whose family had been killed at [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz_concentration_camp "Auschwitz concentration camp"), wrote on 22 June that the work was "so far from the historical truth that the book serves as an apologia for genocide".[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAdler1995-77)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199674-78) On 27 June, Darville wrote in both _The Age_ and _The Sydney Morning Herald_ to defend her book, claiming that the criticism "bordered on the hysterical". She highlighted her supposed direct knowledge of this history, claiming that most of her father's family had been "killed by Jewish Communist Party officials in [Vynnytsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vynnytsia "Vynnytsia")".[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199676%E2%80%9377-79)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDemidenko1995-80) Darville, falsely claiming to be a lawyer,[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenderson1995b-81) also explained that it was her legal training and courtroom experience that had compelled her to "search for a motive" for Ukrainian participation in the Holocaust.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDemidenko1995-80) Darville's defence of her novel appeared alongside a critique from the author [Gerard Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_Henderson "Gerard Henderson"), in which he labelled the novel a "loathsome" book.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenderson1995a-82) That evening, a debate between Darville and Henderson was broadcast on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_/(Australia/) "ABC (Australia)") television.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199678%E2%80%9379-83) An article published that day noted that the growing controversy appeared to be having a positive effect on sales; Allen & Unwin had ordered two reprints, and there were over 3000 back orders.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchanan1995-84) By 11 July, it was reported that the novel had sold more than 10,000 copies and was ninth on the [Angus & Robertson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_%26_Robertson "Angus & Robertson") bestseller list.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVoumard1995-85) On 29 June, the [Harvard Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School") professor [Alan Dershowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Dershowitz "Alan Dershowitz") published an op-ed in both _The Age_ and the _[Australian Financial Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Financial_Review "Australian Financial Review")_ calling the novel "pernicious" and "mean-spirited".[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199679-86) Dershowitz argued that Darville's goal had been to use the novel in furtherance of her opposition to the war crimes trials by justifying Ukrainian participation in the Holocaust in order to ensure that war criminals would go unpunished.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDershowitz1995-87) The antisemitism scholar [Robert S. Wistrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_S._Wistrich "Robert S. Wistrich") weighed into the debate and described the novel's thesis as "more dangerous than any form of Holocaust revisionism".[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMendes199655-88) While criticism of the novel continued to mount, others defended the novel and cast its critics as censorious. An editorial in _The Sydney Morning Herald_ criticised proponents of "[PC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_correctness "Political correctness") fiction".[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTESydney_Morning_Herald1995-89) Marr defended the novel, comparing the "terrible smears and vilification" to the [Satanic Verses controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satanic_Verses_controversy "Satanic Verses controversy").[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1995-90) The author and literary critic [Gerard Windsor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_Windsor "Gerard Windsor") wrote in _Australian Book Review_ that the criticism was a "well-funded witch hunt" filled with "righteous high-mindedness and tribal indignation", while the critic [Morag Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morag_Fraser "Morag Fraser") said that the novel deserved a more serious and tolerant debate.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWindsor1995-91)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFraser1995429-92) Others blamed the Jewish community for the backlash; the conservative columnist [Frank Devine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Devine "Frank Devine") described the criticism as an organised campaign by Jewish organisations, comparing it to the radical feminist campaign against _[The First Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_First_Stone "The First Stone")_.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTENeumann199555-93)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199690-94) ### Darville's identity revealed \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Darville's identity revealed")\] On 19 August 1995 the journalist [David Bentley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bentley_/(journalist/) "David Bentley (journalist)") revealed in _The Courier Mail_ that Helen Demidenko was actually Helen Darville, the daughter of English migrants, and had no Ukrainian ancestry.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199693-95)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019275-96) Bentley had become suspicious of her claims after noticing that Darville had a tendency to provide vague answers when asked about her education, and was informed of her true identity by her high school principal.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199693-95) Bentley was eventually awarded the 1995 [Gold Walkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Walkley "Gold Walkley") for the story.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTECanberra_Times1995-97) At first, many of Darville's defenders refused to believe Bentley's claims. But on 21 August, members of Darville's family publicly confirmed the story.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199694-98) Her brother told the media that her claims of Ukrainian ancestry had been "a great marketing exercise".[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreeman1995-99) Darville released a statement claiming that she had begun to use the name "Demidenko-Darville" at university and that Demidenko was the name of her paternal extended family.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199694-98) It was soon reported that Darville had also pretended to be French and Czech while at university, and that she had committed plagiarism in her university's student newspaper in 1990.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199695-100) On 25 August, a statement with the headline "Helen Darville apologises" was published nationwide. Darville admitted that her Demidenko identity was a fabrication and wrote "I am truly sorry if my book or my actions have been perceived in any way as antisemitic or degrading to the Ukrainian community ... I condemn without reservation the perpetrators of the Holocaust".[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199695%E2%80%9396-101) Following the revelation, criticism mounted towards those who had defended her novel. The literary academic [Ivor Indyk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Indyk "Ivor Indyk") insisted that Darville's ALS Gold Medal should be revoked, while Helen Daniel, the editor of _Australian Book Review_, and [Louise Adler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Adler "Louise Adler"), the arts editor of _The Age_, argued that the judging panel that had awarded Darville the Miles Franklin Award should resign.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996100%E2%80%93101-102) The saga was described in _The Age_ as "perhaps the most shameful literary deception of recent times".[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERundle1995-103) Much of this criticism was directed towards Kitson, who had served on both the Vogel and Miles Franklin judging panels and had been one of the novel's most committed defenders.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERundle1995-103)[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199699-104)[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitchell1996111-105) The historian [William Rubinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rubinstein "William Rubinstein") wrote that Darville had falsified her identity in order to give support to "an antisemitic lie of the most despicable kind", and suggested that the fact that the judging panel had retained their positions was a "sad indictment of Australia's utter provinciality and marginality".[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996102-106) Critics argued that Darville's claims of Ukrainian ancestry had been used to lend credibility to her work. Darville had strongly implied, although she had never explicitly claimed in public, that the work was autobiographical in nature.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTECourtney201982-107)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Connell199642-108)[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeyer200440%E2%80%9341-109) Henderson argued in _The Sydney Morning Herald_ that Darville had received a positive reception because she claimed that her book was drawn from oral history, and that without that excuse, its similarities to antisemitic propaganda became far more glaring.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenderson1995b-81) Bone wrote that she felt some sympathy for Darville, and that most of the blame for the saga should fall on the Miles Franklin judges. Bone expressed her astonishment that the judges had found "a catalogue of atrocities interspersed with some laughably stilted dialogue and some clumsy sex scenes" the best novel of the year.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBone1996-110) Others continued to defend Darville. Devine wrote that the criticism amounted to "miserable, philistine treatment of a young writer of talent".[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996104-111) Kramer, who had served on the Miles Franklin judging panel, wrote that she was puzzled by the "sustained and vitriolic attack on the book and its author", and claimed that the episode "calls into question our claims to be a tolerant and fairminded society".[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996104-111) The philosopher [Peter Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer "Peter Singer") also defended the novel, writing that it was not an antisemitic work and attributing the controversy to the media's tendency to reduce everything to a "kind of sporting contest".[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTESinger1995-112) The new wave of controversy only added to the novel's sales; by 23 August, it was reported that the novel had sold about 25,000 copies.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShenon1995-62)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoberts1995-113) It topped all but one of the _[Weekend Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weekend_Australian "Weekend Australian")_'s biweekly bestseller lists between 1 July and 7 October.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996112-114) ### Plagiarism accusations \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Plagiarism accusations")\] On 26 August, it was reported in the _[Herald Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herald_Sun "Herald Sun")_ that Darville had plagiarised a passage from the novel _[The Power and the Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Power_and_the_Glory "The Power and the Glory")_.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996107-115) The _Sydney Morning Herald_ reported five days later that Darville had plagiarised additional passages from [Thomas Keneally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Keneally "Thomas Keneally")'s novel _[Gossip from the Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gossip_from_the_Forest "Gossip from the Forest")_, [Robin Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Morgan "Robin Morgan")'s _The Demon Lover_, and a Ukrainian collection called _The Black Deeds of the Kremlin_.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996107%E2%80%93108-116) The night before, Allen & Unwin had halted distribution of the book over the plagiarism concerns.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJopson1995b-117) Additional examples of plagiarism in _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ would continue to be reported over the next month.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996108-118) On 7 September, Darville's lawyers at [MinterEllison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MinterEllison "MinterEllison") announced that they believed the plagiarism allegations to be false. The lawyers said that they had consulted an expert on postmodern literature, who had told them that Darville's appropriations from other sources was a normal element of postmodern writing. The lawyers for Allen & Unwin concurred.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996110-119)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGibson1995-120) On 8 September, Allen & Unwin announced that they were "satisfied that allegations of plagiarism cannot be justified" and the novel was returned to distribution.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJopson1995a-121) Eventually Allen & Unwin released a new edition of the book under the name Helen Darville, with the sources copied by Darville now acknowledged and the praise from Marr and Kitson removed from the book's back cover.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996112-114) Commentators were divided on whether the novel contained plagiarism. Indyk said that the plagiarism "attacks the very foundations of the book", while the author [Thomas Shapcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Shapcott "Thomas Shapcott") said that what had occurred was appropriation rather than plagiarism.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJopsonFreeman1995-122) Manne described it as "concealed, pervasive and clumsy plagiarism", although he acknowledged that it did not rise to the level of a breach of copyright law.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996110-119) The literary academic [Judith Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Ryan "Judith Ryan") described Darville's copying as "flagrant", but noted that it did not constitute plagiarism in a legal sense.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERyan2003217-123) [![Image 5: A man in a suit sitting in front of a bookshelf](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Robert_Manne_2001.jpg/250px-Robert_Manne_2001.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Manne_2001.jpg) [Robert Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Manne "Robert Manne"), who emerged as one of the novel's most vocal critics While the novel had somewhat faded from the media spotlight by 1996, the debate continued in academic and literary publications.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShapiro1996b104-124) By February 1996, three books on the saga had been released: an anthology of newspaper articles and television and radio transcripts titled _The Demidenko File;_ a tell-all book by Darville's friend Natalie Jane Prior titled _The Demidenko Diary;_ and a book by Riemer titled _The Demidenko Debate_.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERutherford1996-125) In June, Manne's _The Culture of Forgetting: Helen Demidenko and the Holocaust_ was published.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwood1996-126) Manne was highly critical of the novel, writing, "I found the book laughably inadequate to its subject and unmistakably antisemitic...I found it morally and historically shallow, coarse and cold, even technically quite incompetent".[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne19961-127) Manne argued that no "civilised" European publisher or literary judging panel would have even considered the novel, and that the saga demonstrated the Australian literary establishment's "provincial liberal naivety, historical ignorance and sentimental multiculturalism".[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996188%E2%80%93190-128) Riemer gave a more sympathetic assessment of the novel in _The Demidenko Debate_. He admitted that he was troubled by parts of the novel's subtext, but that he had felt upon his initial reading that the novel was "antisemitic in a limited and on the whole tolerable sense".[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996110%E2%80%93111-129) Riemer defended the novel as a work of fiction, and wrote that its critics' lack of appreciation of the genre led to "many passionate but often ill-founded expressions of outrage".[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199663-130) In a 1997 paper contrasting the reactions of Manne and Riemer, the cultural studies scholar [McKenzie Wark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKenzie_Wark "McKenzie Wark") wrote that Riemer had used the novel to defend an old-fashioned liberal view of tolerance, and to criticise "convenient grand stories" of good and evil.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWark199762%E2%80%9363,_65-131) Riemer and other defenders of the novel argued that much of the fervour had been driven by the Jewish community. He noted that the controversy was strongest in Melbourne, where the Jewish community is more tight-knit and Orthodox than in Sydney.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer1996232%E2%80%93233-132)[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996178-133) In January 1996, a cartoon published in _[The Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Australian "The Australian")_ had shown Darville impaled on a [hanukkiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanukkiah "Hanukkiah"),[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996176%E2%80%93177-134)[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVice2000140%E2%80%93141-135) while Darville herself attributed criticism of her novel to the "Jewish lobby".[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBone1995b-136) Others, however, criticised this claim. Manne noted that the Australian Jewish press was not particularly critical of the novel until after the backlash had already erupted in mainstream newspapers, and that Jewish organisations had played a minimal role in the controversy.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996179%E2%80%93180-137) The journalist [Michael Gawenda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Gawenda "Michael Gawenda") concurred, pointing out that many of the book's fiercest critics were not Jewish, while some of the book's strongest defenders, including Riemer and Singer, were.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGawenda1995-138) Critics of the novel also contested Riemer's suggestion that Darville's opponents had attempted to censor her, insisting that there was no evidence that meaningful threats of legal action against the book were ever made.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996168-139)[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019283-140)[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchaffer1995176-141) ### Motives of Holocaust perpetrators \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Motives of Holocaust perpetrators")\] _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ explores the motivations of Ukrainians like Evheny and Vitaly for collaborating with the Nazis, suggesting that many participated in the Holocaust as retribution for the hardships they had suffered at the hands of Jews under Soviet rule.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199620,_54%E2%80%9355-142)[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorgan2020374%E2%80%93375-143) In an interview on [ABC Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Broadcasting_Corporation#Radio "Australian Broadcasting Corporation"), Darville explained that her goal had been "not to take the Holocaust out of the context of European history, and so to make my readers appreciate that it's a facet, and probably a fairly inevitable facet of European history at that time".[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996161-144) Fiona explains that the suffering of Ukrainians and the suffering of Jews were intimately tied together, saying that "the Ukrainian famine bled into the Holocaust and one fed the other".[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFraser1995421-145) In the pre-war years, Jews are shown to be responsible for many of the Kovalenko family's sufferings, including the deaths of Vitaly's father and infant brother.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996151-146) The novel then depicts the lives of the Ukrainian guards at Treblinka as they exact their revenge on those they view as responsible for this suffering, showing the guards to be largely content and free of guilt.[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199619%E2%80%9320-147) In a review of the novel published in _Australian Book Review,_ Harboe-Ree writes that the novel can be understood to be presenting the case for the defendants in the trials of Nazi war criminals by arguing that collaborators like Evheny committed their crimes only due to the extreme provocation they had suffered.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarboe-Ree1994-51) Scholars and reviewers have also pointed out that the narrative places its focus on the humanity of Ukrainian collaborators, at times shifting the reader's sympathy away from their Jewish victims, by emphasising the injustices committed against Ukrainians by Jews and communists.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarboe-Ree1994-51)[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996135-148)[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVice2000193-149) Wark suggests that the novel "opens a crack in the grand fables of the early 20th century and lets a little late 20th century scepticism in" by depicting the Holocaust's perpetrators as flawed humans and questioning the narrative of their absolute evil.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWark199763-150) ### Responsibility and forgiveness \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Responsibility and forgiveness")\] The novel also explores the moral responsibility of Nazi collaborators and suggests a need to forgive rather than prosecute wartime atrocities.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996116-151) Darville was a strong critic of the trials of former Nazi war criminals, and said that she had been motivated to write the novel by the upcoming trial of Ivan Polyukhovich and by her belief that the prosecutions of Nazi collaborators were motivated by a desire for revenge.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019286-16)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199622-26) The novel features the redemption or rehabilitation of some Holocaust perpetrators; one SS officer becomes an anti-racist and joins the [Peace Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Corps "Peace Corps") after the war, while Ivan the Terrible's brutality is explained to have been caused by the death of his family at the hands of Jews.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorgan2020373%E2%80%93374-152)[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996122%E2%80%93123-153) Vitaly explains to Fiona that until the war crimes prosecution he had stopped hating Jews, and that he is trying to feel sorry for what he did.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996117-154) The academic Peter Christoff writes that the novel presents Ukrainian Nazi collaborators as "passive, coerced innocents" who cannot fairly be held responsible for their actions.[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristoff199546-155) _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ is widely regarded as an example of postmodern literature. Its writing is characterised by a lack of explicit or implied authorial commentary, and by the use of detached, unemotional prose.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorley200784-156)[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith201969-157)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShapiro1996a47-158) Its detached style has been described as an embrace of the [amoral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorality "Amorality") character of postmodern literature.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShapiro1996b106-159)[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShapiro1996b113-160) Riemer describes the novel as exemplifying the "loss of faith in the authorial voice" and the "essential scepticism and tendency towards irony" that characterise late-20th century literature, while the philosopher [Raimond Gaita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raimond_Gaita "Raimond Gaita") writes that this lack of authorial voice provides the reader with little moral guidance in understanding the horrors that the novel describes.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiemer199632%E2%80%9333,_36-161)[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGaita199533-162) Ryan believes that the anachronisms of both Darville's novel and her performance as Helen Demidenko reveal that she was instead attempting a [pastiche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastiche "Pastiche") of postmodernism; she concludes that the novel represents a "thought-provoking yet ultimately confused attempt" at examining the techniques of postmodern literature.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTERyan2003183-163) The significance of the authorial voice in _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ has been widely debated. Sue Vice, a scholar of Holocaust fiction, writes that the novel is constructed "idiosyncratically" through a combination of first-person accounts from Fiona, Kateryna and Vitaly, and an implied third-person narration.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVice2000149-164) This was viewed by some readers as a technical flaw in the novel's construction.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne199639,_44-165)[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVice2000194-166) The author Serge Liberman writes that the lack of a clear authorial voice creates a "near-schizoid dissociation" between Vitaly and Kateryna's recounting of the Holocaust's horrors and the narrator's lack of condemnation.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTELiberman1995168%E2%80%93169-167) The identity of the implied third-person narrator has been subject to multiple interpretations; some readers regarded the third-person voice as being that of Fiona, while others believe that it represents the voice of the author.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996125%E2%80%93129,_182-168)[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKirkpatrick1995158%E2%80%93260-169) In 2000, Vice defended the novel by arguing that it was an example of "[polyphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphony_/(literature/) "Polyphony (literature)")", or a dialogue in which the narrator does not have an omniscient perspective.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVice2000149%E2%80%93150-170) Vice concluded that the novel "testifies to the great power and potential of the polyphonic novel and [dialogized heteroglossia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteroglossia#Dialogized_Heteroglossia "Heteroglossia")" in writing fiction about the Holocaust.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVice2000159-171) In 2007, however, Vice wrote that she no longer believed that the novel was an example of genuine polyphony, and that multivocality was instead used to disguise its author's agenda and her tendency towards "sexualising and glamorising" the Holocaust's perpetrators.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVice2007178%E2%80%93180-172) The novel and its reception have been widely analysed as a case study in [Australian multiculturalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiculturalism_in_Australia "Multiculturalism in Australia"). The literary scholar [Sneja Gunew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sneja_Gunew "Sneja Gunew") argues that the episode illustrates the ways in which "multicultural" authors are often read simplistically and are valued largely for their "authenticity".[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGunew1996b57%E2%80%9359-173)[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGunew1996a8-174) Zora Simic argues that by presenting herself as Demidenko, Darville inadvertently produced a critique of the ethnic [essentialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essentialism "Essentialism") of Australian literature.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimic200739%E2%80%9340-175) Jane Hyde echoes this sentiment, arguing it is unsurprising that a young person growing up in an environment where multiculturalism was increasingly central to Australian life would seek to adopt a marginalised ethnic identity.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHyde199549-176) The Holocaust scholar [Avril Alba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avril_Alba "Avril Alba") suggests that the novel's reception also revealed the "shaky foundations" of Australian multiculturalism during the 1990s, reflecting the tension between those who believed that it was important to forget and reconcile past injustices, and those who believed that this forgetting would undermine Australia's commitment to building a just and diverse society.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlba2019273-177) Many critics of the novel also argued that its success demonstrated a concerning lack of historical literacy regarding the Holocaust. Christoff writes that European publishers would have immediately recognised the novel as a "shallow, immature and ultimately antisemitic novel" unsuitable for publication.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristoff199548-178) Manne concurs, arguing that the novel "revives as 'history' the Nazi myth of Jewish Bolshevism" and that European publishers would have rightly rejected it.[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996187%E2%80%93188-179) More recent scholarship has also pointed out that while applying the techniques of postmodern literature to the Holocaust was once seen as fundamentally inappropriate, _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ was part of a wider trend of increasingly adventurous literary works about the Holocaust, including those that provide a more sympathetic or nuanced portrayal of its perpetrators.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorgan20208-180)[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShields201666%E2%80%9367-181) Shapcott had regarded this as an ominous trend, writing that _The Hand That Signed the Paper_ was the product of "a new generation which is distant from the horrors of the Holocaust, who see it as something they want to question, or to challenge, or to set aside".[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hand_That_Signed_the_Paper#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManne1996133-182) * [1994 in Australian
